blocks.text: 今天我们发布Old Ideas, Novel Problems，这是一项关于大语言模型评估科学研究想法新颖性的可靠程度的新研究。除论文外，我们还发布了一个用于测试新颖性评判器的基准、数据和代码，以及一个研究人员可用于构建新评估集的自动化流水线。

inlines.text: 今天我们发布
Old Ideas, Novel Problems
，这是一项关于大语言模型评估科学研究想法新颖性的可靠程度的新研究。除论文外，我们还发布了一个用于测试新颖性评判器的基准、数据和代码，以及一个研究人员可用于构建新评估集的自动化流水线。

blocks.text: 在Ai2，我们一直在开发支持科学发现不同环节的AI系统。DataVoyager帮助研究人员探索和分析结构化数据，AutoDiscovery生成并检验假设，Theorizer将大量文献中的证据综合为候选科学理论。与Asta一起，这些项目指向了能够帮助研究人员从理解已有工作，走向提出、检验和完善新想法的系统。

blocks.text: 但生成研究想法只是自动化科学发现挑战的一部分。这些想法还需要贡献真正新颖的内容，这意味着这些系统需要一种方法来区分新颖方向与主要只是重新包装已有工作的方向。

inlines.text: 但生成研究想法只是自动化科学发现挑战的一部分。这些想法还需要贡献真正新颖的内容，这意味着这些系统需要一种方法来区分新颖方向与主要只是重新包装已有工作的方向。

blocks.text: 这一判断通常被交给另一个LLM——我们称之为新颖性评判器。新颖性评判器评估一个研究想法相对于已有工作是否新颖，可以单独评估，也可以与另一个想法比较。构建评判器没有标准方法；研究团队会选择模型、提示词、评估格式、推理预算，有时还会选择文献检索系统。这些选择可能对判定结果产生实质性影响。然而，这些评判器往往只在人类撰写的论文上验证，而不是在它们实际要评估的AI生成想法上验证。

inlines.text: 这一判断通常被交给另一个LLM——我们称之为
新颖性评判器
。新颖性评判器评估一个研究想法相对于已有工作是否新颖，可以单独评估，也可以与另一个想法比较。构建评判器没有标准方法；研究团队会选择模型、提示词、评估格式、推理预算，有时还会选择文献检索系统。这些选择可能对判定结果产生实质性影响。然而，这些评判器往往只在人类撰写的论文上验证，而不是在它们实际要评估的AI生成想法上验证。

blocks.text: 我们的新基准结果表明，新颖性评估本身远不可靠。在六个LLM评判器——GPT-5.1、GPT-5.2、GPT-5.4、Claude Sonnet 4.5、Claude Opus 4.5和Claude Opus 4.6——中，评估设置看似微小的变化会对相同想法产生截然不同的判断。在一项实验中，仅改变提示词中的几个词，模型在识别两个想法中哪个更新颖时的准确率就变化超过50个百分点。检索和额外推理并不能持续改善判断，而两个专门构建的新颖性评估系统表现还不如一个简单提示的Claude Opus 4.6基线。

blocks.text: 如果AI要在科学发现中发挥更大作用，我们需要更可靠的方法来判断它是否真的提出了新东西。我们的工作为研究这一问题提供了工具，同时表明还有多少问题尚未解决。

blocks.text: 构建新颖性评判器基准

inlines.text: 构建新颖性评判器基准

blocks.text: 为了测试新颖性评判器区分更新颖与较不新颖研究想法的可靠程度，我们首先需要一些例子，这些例子中关于底层科学贡献的原创性有强有力的证据。

inlines.text: 为了测试新颖性评判器区分更新颖与较不新颖研究想法的可靠程度，我们首先需要一些例子，这些例子中关于底层科学贡献的原创性有强有力的证据。

blocks.text: 因此，我们围绕 ICLR 2026 同行评审构建了一条自动化流水线。我们没有把论文被接收当作新颖性的代理指标，而是直接从评审意见本身中挖掘评审人明确讨论某项贡献原创性的段落。这一区分至关重要；一篇论文即使新颖性并不突出，只要在其他方面足够扎实，也可能被接收。同样，一篇被拒的论文即使贡献具有原创性，也可能存在其他弱点。

inlines.text: 因此，我们围绕 ICLR 2026 同行评审构建了一条自动化流水线。我们没有把论文被接收当作新颖性的代理指标，而是直接从评审意见本身中挖掘评审人明确讨论某项贡献原创性的段落。这一区分至关重要；一篇论文即使新颖性并不突出，只要在其他方面足够扎实，也可能被接收。同样，一篇被拒的论文即使贡献具有原创性，也可能存在其他弱点。

blocks.text: 我们构建了一个高新颖性池，包含 154 个人类撰写的研究想法：选取在其 ICLR 研究领域中评分排名前 10% 的被接收论文，且评审人明确肯定其新颖性、没有任何评审人对此提出异议。我们采用相反的标准构建了较低新颖性池：从排名后 10% 的被拒论文中选取 145 个想法，其评审人提出了原创性方面的担忧，且没有任何评审人明确肯定其新颖性。在对评审挖掘流程的单独检查中，一位标注者在 50 个案例中的 47 个上认同了所提取新颖性信号的极性；所有分歧都不会改变某位评审人是否被计为赞扬或质疑该论文新颖性的判断。

blocks.text: 这两个池共同构成了我们的第一个评估设置——仅人类，用于检验新颖性评判者能否区分有强证据表明新颖性较高或较低的人类撰写想法。但在实践中，新颖性评判者正越来越多地被用于评估 AI 生成的想法。因此我们创建了第二个设置——人类+生成。

inlines.text: 这两个池共同构成了我们的第一个评估设置——
仅人类
，用于检验新颖性评判者能否区分有强证据表明新颖性较高或较低的人类撰写想法。但在实践中，新颖性评判者正越来越多地被用于评估 AI 生成的想法。因此我们创建了第二个设置——
人类+生成

blocks.text: 对于这个池，我们将同样的 154 个经过验证的人类想法与一个简单 LLM 生成器产生的 154 个想法配对。我们假设生成的想法不如人类撰写的对应想法新颖；这些是弱标签，并非对每个想法都经过验证的判断。生成器只收到一个研究领域和一条提出新颖想法的指令，没有文献检索、工具、迭代或反馈。这为我们提供了一个保守的比较：一边是基础生成器产生的想法，另一边是评审人明确认可其原创性的 ICLR 前 10% 论文贡献。

inlines.text: 对于这个池，我们将同样的 154 个经过验证的人类想法与一个简单 LLM 生成器产生的 154 个想法配对。我们假设生成的想法不如人类撰写的对应想法新颖；这些是弱标签，并非对每个想法都经过验证的判断。生成器只收到一个研究领域和一条提出新颖想法的指令，没有文献检索、工具、迭代或反馈。这为我们提供了一个保守的比较：一边是基础生成器产生的想法，另一边是评审人明确认可其原创性的 ICLR 前 10% 论文贡献。

blocks.text: 作为额外检查，一位专家独立审阅了 30 对人类+生成配对，这些配对严重偏向我们最强评判者判断错误的案例；我们还将人类和 AI 生成的想法改写为统一结构，以检验评判者是否只是在反应写作风格上的差异。该专家在全部 30 对中都更偏好人类想法，并认为没有任何生成的想法具有新颖性。

blocks.text: 重要的是，我们的许多核心发现根本不依赖于这些标签。如果两个合理的评估设置对同一对想法给出相反答案，这种分歧本身就揭示了不稳定性。

blocks.text: 微小的变化可能产生截然不同的判定

inlines.text: 微小的变化可能产生截然不同的判定

blocks.text: 利用我们收集的人类撰写和 AI 生成的研究想法，我们测试了六个 LLM 评判者——GPT-5.1、GPT-5.2、GPT-5.4、Claude Sonnet 4.5、Claude Opus 4.5 和 Claude Opus 4.6——通过逐点（即绝对新颖性评分）和成对（即比较两个想法以找出更新颖者）两种比较方式评估新颖性的能力。我们每次只改变一个因素：提示词、推理预算、评判者能否看到相关论文、想法的格式、将多少次判断合并为最终裁决，以及——对于 AI 生成的想法——由哪个模型生成。

inlines.text: 利用我们收集的人类撰写和 AI 生成的研究想法，我们测试了六个 LLM 评判者——GPT-5.1、GPT-5.2、GPT-5.4、Claude Sonnet 4.5、Claude Opus 4.5 和 Claude Opus 4.6——通过逐点（即绝对新颖性评分）和成对（即比较两个想法以找出更新颖者）两种比较方式评估新颖性的能力。我们每次只改变一个因素：提示词、推理预算、评判者能否看到相关论文、想法的格式、将多少次判断合并为最终裁决，以及——对于 AI 生成的想法——由哪个模型生成。

blocks.text: 性能的最大变化来自我们如何提示模型判断新颖性。

inlines.text: 性能的最大变化来自我们如何提示模型判断新颖性。

blocks.text: 例如，我们向 GPT-5.4 展示了相同的 Human+Generated 配对——每对包含一个经过验证的人类撰写的想法和一个 AI 生成的想法——并使用了两种提示词。其中一种提示词告诉模型，评审者发现每对中恰好有一个想法是新颖的，并要求它指出是哪一个；另一种则只是简单地问哪个想法是新颖的。当我们改用更简单的提示词时，准确率从 93.5% 下降到 40.9%——低于随机水平——并且模型对超过一半的相同配对改变了判定。

Human+Generated
配对——每对包含一个经过验证的人类撰写的想法和一个 AI 生成的想法——并使用了两种提示词。其中一种提示词告诉模型，评审者发现每对中恰好有一个想法是新颖的，并要求它指出是哪一个；另一种则只是简单地问哪个想法是新颖的。当我们改用更简单的提示词时，准确率从 93.5% 下降到 40.9%——低于随机水平——并且模型对超过一半的相同配对改变了判定。

blocks.text: 相比之下，同样的提示词变化在 Human-Only 数据集上仅使准确率变化了约七个百分点，该数据集将人类撰写的想法与更强和更弱的新颖性证据配对。这表明，新颖性评判器在人类撰写的研究上可能表现得相对稳定，但在 AI 生成的想法上却可能表现得很不相同。

blocks.text: 尽管如此，人类撰写的想法也并非不受影响。我们在 Human-Only 数据集上也看到了显著的变化；同样的改动使 Claude Opus 4.6 的准确率变化了 21 个百分点。只是这些变化没有在 AI 生成的想法上那么严重。

blocks.text: 也不存在普遍更好的提示词。例如，在逐个评判想法时，去掉一条警告评判者不要将琐碎或渐进式贡献视为新颖的指令，提高了某些评判者的准确率，却降低了另一些评判者的准确率。换句话说，对某个模型有效的提示词可能无法迁移到另一个模型。

blocks.text: 我们还测试了新颖性评判器的一种常见用途：比较来自两个 AI 生成器的想法。我们将 Claude Opus 4.5 与 Claude Sonnet 4.5 的想法配对，将 GPT-5.4 与 GPT-5.1 的想法配对。在所测试的提示词变化中，六位评判者平均约有四分之一到三分之一的判定发生了改变。这种分歧可以在不假设哪个生成器产生更新颖想法的情况下被测量，从而表明评判者提示词的选择如何影响创意生成系统之间的比较。

inlines.text: 我们还测试了新颖性评判器的一种常见用途：比较来自两个 AI 生成器的想法。我们将 Claude Opus 4.5 与 Claude Sonnet 4.5 的想法配对，将 GPT-5.4 与 GPT-5.1 的想法配对。在所测试的提示词变化中，六位评判者平均约有四分之一到三分之一的判定发生了改变。这种分歧可以在不假设哪个生成器产生更新颖想法的情况下被测量，从而表明评判者提示词的选择如何影响创意生成系统之间的比较。

blocks.text: 更多的搜索和推理并不一定产生更好的新颖性判断。我们给 GPT-5.6 Sol 分配了超高的推理预算，并限制在 arXiv 上进行实时迭代搜索，然后将其与标准检索评判者进行比较，后者各自看到五篇预先检索的摘要。（此比较中的所有评判者在 Human+Generated 上对每个想法各运行一次。）该智能体评判者得分为 0.78 macro-F1——比 Claude Opus 4.6 的 0.89 低 11 个百分点，与更简单的 Claude Opus 4.5 和 GPT-5.4 设置大致处于同一区间——而按当前 API 价格计算，每次决策的成本约为后者的 10 倍。（在此语境下，macro-F1 衡量评判者识别新颖和非新颖想法的能力；越高越好。）

blocks.text: 专用评估器也没有更准确，尽管成本高得多。在 Human+Generated 集上，一个使用低推理和三次调用多数投票的简单 Claude Opus 4.6 提示词在总评估成本为 2.59 美元的情况下达到了 0.854 macro-F1。相比之下，Idea Novelty Checker——一个基于文献的检索与重排序流水线——得分为 0.642，成本为 30.66 美元；而 Sakana AI 的 AI Scientist——其新颖性评估器迭代搜索 Semantic Scholar——得分为 0.772，成本为 82.05 美元。（两个专用评估器均使用 Claude Opus 4.6，每次决策调用一次。）

blocks.text: 我们的结果表明，基于大语言模型的新颖性评估仍是一个重大的开放问题。在人类撰写的研究上表现可靠的评审模型，面对 AI 生成的想法时可能表现不同；对某个模型有效的提示词，可能对另一个模型有害；更多的搜索或算力并不必然带来更一致的判断。

blocks.text: Today we’re releasing Old Ideas, Novel Problems, a new study of how reliably large language models can evaluate the novelty of scientific research ideas. Alongside the paper, we’re publishing a benchmark, data, and code for testing novelty judges, plus an automated pipeline researchers can use to build new evaluation sets.

inlines.text: Today we’re releasing
Old Ideas, Novel Problems

, a new study of how reliably large language models can evaluate the novelty of scientific research ideas. Alongside the paper, we’re publishing a benchmark, data, and code for testing novelty judges, plus an automated pipeline researchers can use to build new evaluation sets.

blocks.text: At Ai2, we’ve been developing AI systems that support different parts of scientific discovery. DataVoyager helps researchers explore and analyze structured data, AutoDiscovery generates and tests hypotheses, and Theorizer synthesizes evidence across large bodies of literature into candidate scientific theories. Together with Asta, these projects point toward systems that can help researchers move from understanding prior work to proposing, testing, and refining new ideas.

blocks.text: But generating research ideas is only part of the challenge of automating scientific discovery. Those ideas also need to contribute something genuinely new, which means these systems need a way to distinguish a novel direction from one that mostly repackages existing work.

inlines.text: But generating research ideas is only part of the challenge of automating scientific discovery. Those ideas also need to contribute something genuinely new, which means these systems need a way to distinguish a novel direction from one that mostly repackages existing work.

blocks.text: That judgment is often handed to another LLM—what we call a novelty judge. Novelty judges assess whether a research idea is new relative to prior work, either on its own or in comparison with another idea. There’s no standard way to build one; research teams choose a model, prompt, evaluation format, reasoning budget, and sometimes a literature-retrieval system. Those choices can materially affect the verdict. Yet these judges are often validated only on human-written papers rather than the AI-generated ideas they are actually meant to evaluate.

novelty judge

. Novelty judges assess whether a research idea is new relative to prior work, either on its own or in comparison with another idea. There’s no standard way to build one; research teams choose a model, prompt, evaluation format, reasoning budget, and sometimes a literature-retrieval system. Those choices can materially affect the verdict. Yet these judges are often validated only on human-written papers rather than the AI-generated ideas they are actually meant to evaluate.

blocks.text: Our new benchmark results suggest novelty evaluation itself is far from reliable. Across six LLM judges – GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.6 – seemingly small changes to the evaluation setup produce dramatically different judgments of the same ideas. In one experiment, changing just a few words in a prompt shifts a model’s accuracy in identifying which of two ideas is more novel by more than 50 percentage points. Retrieval and additional reasoning do not consistently improve judgments, and two purpose-built novelty evaluation systems perform worse than a simple prompted Claude Opus 4.6 baseline.

blocks.text: If AI is going to play a larger role in scientific discovery, we need more dependable ways to tell whether it is actually proposing something new. Our work provides tools for studying that problem, while showing how much remains unresolved.

blocks.text: Building a benchmark for novelty judges

inlines.text: Building a benchmark for novelty judges

blocks.text: To test how reliably novelty judges can distinguish more novel research ideas from less novel ones, we first needed examples where there was strong evidence about the originality of the underlying scientific contribution.

inlines.text: To test how reliably novelty judges can distinguish more novel research ideas from less novel ones, we first needed examples where there was strong evidence about the originality of the underlying scientific contribution.

blocks.text: So we built an automated pipeline around ICLR 2026 peer reviews. Rather than treating paper acceptance as a proxy for novelty, we mined the reviews themselves for passages where reviewers explicitly discussed a contribution’s originality. That distinction is key; a paper can be accepted without being particularly novel as long as it is strong enough in other aspects. Likewise, a rejected paper with an original contribution can have other weaknesses.

inlines.text: So we built an automated pipeline around ICLR 2026 peer reviews. Rather than treating paper acceptance as a proxy for novelty, we mined the reviews themselves for passages where reviewers explicitly discussed a contribution’s originality. That distinction is key; a paper can be accepted without being particularly novel as long as it is strong enough in other aspects. Likewise, a rejected paper with an original contribution can have other weaknesses.

blocks.text: We created a high-novelty pool of 154 human-authored research ideas by selecting accepted papers in the top-rated 10% of their ICLR research area whose reviewers positively identified novelty and where no reviewer disputed it. We applied the reverse criteria to build a lower-novelty pool: 145 ideas from rejected papers in the bottom 10% whose reviewers raised originality concerns without any reviewer positively identifying novelty. In a separate check of the review-mining process, an annotator agreed with the extracted novelty-signal polarity in 47 of 50 cases; none of the disagreements would have changed whether a reviewer was counted as praising or disputing the paper’s novelty.

blocks.text: Together, these two pools form our first evaluation setting, Human-Only, which tests whether novelty judges can tell apart human-authored ideas with strong evidence of higher or lower novelty. But in practice, novelty judges are increasingly being used to evaluate AI-generated ideas. So we created a second setting, Human+Generated.

Human+Generated

blocks.text: For this pool, we paired the same 154 validated human ideas with 154 ideas produced by a simple LLM generator. We assumed the generated ideas were less novel than their human-authored counterparts; these are weak labels, not verified judgments for every idea. The generator received only a research area and an instruction to propose a novel idea, with no literature search, tools, iteration, or feedback. This gave us a conservative comparison between ideas from a basic generator and contributions from top-10% ICLR papers whose reviewers had explicitly endorsed their originality.

blocks.text: As additional checks, an expert independently reviewed 30 Human+Generated pairs, heavily weighted toward cases our strongest judge got wrong, and we rewrote the human- and AI-generated ideas into a common structure to test whether judges were simply reacting to differences in writing style. The expert preferred the human idea in all 30 pairs and judged none of the generated ideas novel.

blocks.text: Small changes can produce very different verdicts

inlines.text: Small changes can produce very different verdicts

blocks.text: Using our collections of human-authored and AI-generated research ideas, we tested how well six LLM judges – GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.6 – could evaluate novelty through both pointwise (i.e., absolute novelty ratings) and pairwise (i.e., comparing two ideas to find the most novel) comparisons. We varied one factor at a time: the prompt, reasoning budget, whether the judge could see related papers, how the ideas were formatted, how many judgments were combined into a final verdict, and – for AI-generated ideas – which model generated them.

We varied one factor at a time: the prompt, reasoning budget, whether the judge could see related papers, how the ideas were formatted, how many judgments were combined into a final verdict, and – for AI-generated ideas – which model generated them.

blocks.text: The largest shifts in performance came from how we prompted the model to judge novelty.

inlines.text: The largest shifts in performance came from how we prompted the model to judge novelty.

blocks.text: For example, we showed GPT-5.4 the same Human+Generated pairs – each containing one validated human-authored idea and one AI-generated idea – with two prompts. One prompt told the model that reviewers had found exactly one idea in each pair to be novel and asked it to identify which one; the other simply asked which idea was novel. When we switched to the simpler prompt, accuracy dropped from 93.5% to 40.9% – below chance – and the model changed its verdict on more than half of the same pairs.

blocks.text: By contrast, the same prompt change shifted accuracy by only about seven percentage points on the Human-Only dataset, which pairs human-authored ideas with stronger and weaker evidence of novelty. That suggests a novelty judge can appear relatively stable on human-authored research but behave very differently on AI-generated ideas.

blocks.text: There was also no universally better prompt. For example, when judging ideas individually, dropping an instruction that warned judges not to treat trivial or incremental contributions as novel improved accuracy for some judges while reducing it for others. A prompt that works well for one model may not transfer to another, in other words.

blocks.text: We also tested a common use of novelty judges: comparing ideas from two AI generators. We paired ideas from Claude Opus 4.5 with Claude Sonnet 4.5, and GPT-5.4 with GPT-5.1. Across the tested prompt changes, roughly a quarter to a third of verdicts changed on average across six judges. This disagreement can be measured without assuming which generator produces more novel ideas, showing how the choice of judge prompt can affect comparisons between ideation systems.

blocks.text: More search and reasoning didn’t necessarily produce better novelty judgments. We gave GPT-5.6 Sol an extra-high reasoning budget and live, iterative search restricted to arXiv, then compared it with standard-retrieval judges that each saw five pre-retrieved abstracts. (All judges in this comparison ran once per idea on Human+Generated.) The agentic judge scored 0.78 macro-F1 – 11 points behind Claude Opus 4.6 at 0.89, and in roughly the same range as simpler Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.4 setups – while costing roughly 10× more per decision at current API prices. (In this context, macro-F1 measures how well a judge identifies novel and non-novel ideas; higher is better.)

blocks.text: Purpose-built evaluators weren’t more accurate either, despite costing substantially more. On the Human+Generated set, a simple Claude Opus 4.6 prompt using low reasoning and majority voting across three calls achieved 0.854 macro-F1 at a total evaluation cost of $2.59. By comparison, Idea Novelty Checker, a literature-grounded retrieval and reranking pipeline, scored 0.642 at $30.66, while Sakana AI’s AI Scientist, whose novelty evaluator iteratively searches Semantic Scholar, scored 0.772 at $82.05. (Both dedicated evaluators used Claude Opus 4.6, with one call per decision.)

blocks.text: Toward more reliable evaluation of novel research

inlines.text: Toward more reliable evaluation of novel research

blocks.text: Our results suggest that LLM-based novelty evaluation remains a major open problem. Judges that appear reliable on human-authored research may behave differently on AI-generated ideas; prompts that help one model can hurt another; and more search or compute does not necessarily produce more consistent judgments.

inlines.text: Our results suggest that LLM-based novelty evaluation remains a major open problem. Judges that appear reliable on human-authored research may behave differently on AI-generated ideas; prompts that help one model can hurt another; and more search or compute does not necessarily produce more consistent judgments.

blocks.text: Future work should test judges on the kinds of ideas they will actually evaluate, measure sensitivity across prompts and models, improve how prior literature is incorporated, and build benchmarks that can evolve as the scientific literature grows and AI systems improve. Our benchmark and reusable data pipeline are a starting point—researchers can apply them to new peer reviews, other scientific communities, and future generations of novelty judges.

blocks.text: Automated ideation depends on more than generating plausible research directions; we also need ways to tell when those ideas are genuinely new. By making the weaknesses of current novelty judges easier to measure, we hope this release helps researchers build more robust ways to evaluate AI-generated research ideas.
